sections.skill: Compute effective hourly rates and recognize capacity limits

questions.prompt: A job earns 120 dollars of profit and takes 4 hours in total. What is the effective hourly rate?
questions.intro: An owner's time is limited, so it has a cost. CAPACITY is the most work the business can do in a period. If an owner can work 30 hours a week on paid tasks, that is her capacity. To find an effective HOURLY RATE, divide profit from a job by the total hours it takes, including travel, emails, invoices and setup, not just the visible work. A price that looks high can become a low hourly rate. When capacity is full, serving more customers safely takes qualified help or a better process. Raising prices is a separate choice: it manages demand and earns more per job, but it does not add capacity.

questions.prompt: A full bus is like what?
questions.intro: A bus has a fixed number of seats. Once they are full, no more people can ride that trip, no matter how many wait. An owner's week is like the bus: it has a fixed number of working hours. Each job takes some seats, including the "hidden" seats for travel and paperwork. When the hours are full, a bigger bus (help) or more trips (more hours) carry more riders. A pricier ticket (higher prices) adds no seats, but it changes who rides and earns more per seat.
